An alga (plural: algae) is a living organism that makes its own food using sunlight — similar to how plants do — but it is not a plant. It is a simpler, more ancient form of life that lives mostly in water.

Think of the green, slimy coating you sometimes see on the surface of a pond, on wet rocks, or on the walls of an aquarium. That is algae. The green, brown, or red seaweed you see washed up on a beach? Also algae.
What Exactly Is an Alga?

An alga is a photosynthetic organism. "Photosynthetic" simply means it captures energy from sunlight and uses it to produce its own food (a sugar) from water and carbon dioxide — a process called photosynthesis. As a byproduct of this process, it releases oxygen into the environment.

Algae are classified as eukaryotes, which means their cells have a proper nucleus (a central control unit enclosed in a membrane). This makes them more complex than bacteria, but far simpler than plants or animals in terms of their overall body structure.
How Is an Alga Different from a Plant?

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand. Algae and plants both photosynthesize, but they are fundamentally different in structure:

  • A plant has true roots, stems, and leaves — specialized organs that perform specific jobs (absorbing water, transporting nutrients, etc.).
  • An alga has none of these. Its body (called a thallus) is a much simpler structure without those specialized organs. It has no vascular system — no internal "plumbing" to transport water and nutrients from one part to another.
  • Plants reproduce using seeds, flowers, or cones. Algae use simpler methods — spores, cell division, or fragmentation (breaking off a piece that grows into a new individual).
  • Plants live on land (though some grow near or in water). Algae are primarily aquatic — they thrive in water.

In short: plants are sophisticated, land-adapted organisms with complex internal anatomy. Algae are simpler, mostly water-dwelling organisms that lack that complex anatomy.
The Incredible Size Range

One of the most striking things about algae is how wildly different they can be in size:

  • Some algae are single-celled and completely invisible to the naked eye. These microscopic algae (like diatoms and dinoflagellates) float in oceans and lakes as part of what is called phytoplankton — tiny floating organisms that form the base of most aquatic food chains.
  • Others are multicellular and can be enormous. Giant kelp, for example, is a type of alga that can grow over 45 meters (150 feet) long, forming vast underwater forests.

So the word "alga" covers a breathtaking range — from a single invisible cell to a towering underwater giant.
Algae Are Not One Unified Family

Here is a subtlety that even many educated people miss: algae are not a single natural group in the way that, say, mammals are. Different types of algae actually evolved independently from different ancestors. Scientists call this being polyphyletic.

What they all share is the function — they all photosynthesize and live primarily in water — but they are not all closely related to each other. The major groups include:

  • Green algae — the most plant-like; believed to be the ancestors of all land plants
  • Red algae — found mostly in warm, tropical oceans; used in cooking and food production (e.g., nori, the seaweed wrapper used in sushi)
  • Brown algae — includes large seaweeds and kelp; found in cold ocean waters
  • Diatoms — microscopic, single-celled algae with intricate glass-like cell walls made of silica; incredibly abundant in oceans
  • Dinoflagellates — single-celled, often found in the ocean; some are bioluminescent (they glow in the dark); some produce toxins that cause "red tides"
A Word on "Blue-Green Algae"

You may hear the term blue-green algae. Despite the name, these are not true algae at all. They are actually a type of bacteria called cyanobacteria. They are prokaryotes — their cells lack a proper nucleus — which places them in an entirely different category of life. They do photosynthesize, which is why they were historically grouped with algae, but modern science is clear: they are bacteria, not algae. The name "blue-green algae" is a historical holdover that stuck in common language.
Where Do Algae Live?

While water is their primary home, algae are surprisingly adaptable:

  • Oceans and seas — both on the surface and in shallow coastal zones
  • Freshwater — lakes, rivers, ponds, streams
  • Soil — certain algae live in and on moist soil
  • Snow and ice — some algae survive in polar or high-altitude snow, turning it pink or red (known as "watermelon snow")
  • On tree bark, rocks, and walls — in damp environments
  • Inside other organisms — some algae live symbiotically inside corals, providing corals with food through photosynthesis in exchange for shelter and nutrients. When corals are stressed and expel these algae, the coral "bleaches" and turns white — a serious environmental problem.
Why Algae Matter Enormously

Algae are not just pond slime — they are critically important to life on Earth:

1. Oxygen production: It is estimated that algae (primarily oceanic phytoplankton) produce roughly 50% of all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. Every second breath you take is thanks to algae.

2. Foundation of aquatic food chains: Microscopic algae are eaten by tiny animals (zooplankton), which are eaten by small fish, which are eaten by larger fish, and so on. Without algae, aquatic food webs would collapse.

3. Carbon capture: Algae absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during photosynthesis, playing a key role in regulating Earth's climate.

4. Human uses: Algae are used as food (seaweed in Asian cuisines), as a source of ingredients in ice cream, salad dressings, and cosmetics (via compounds called carrageenan and agar), in medicine, and are being researched as a source of biofuel — a sustainable alternative to fossil fuels.
Algal Blooms — When Algae Become a Problem

Under normal conditions, algae are beneficial. But when conditions are right — usually an excess of nutrients (like fertilizers from farmland washing into water) combined with warm temperatures — algae can multiply explosively. This is called an algal bloom.

Blooms can block sunlight from reaching deeper water, depleting oxygen and killing fish. Some blooms are toxic, producing poisons that are deadly to animals and harmful to humans. The famous "red tide" is a type of harmful algal bloom caused by certain dinoflagellates.
Singular vs. Plural — A Quick Note

• Alga = singular (one organism or one species being referred to as a unit)
  • Algae = plural (multiple organisms or types)

In everyday speech, people almost always say "algae" even in contexts where "alga" would technically be correct. "Algae" has become so dominant that it functions as both singular and plural in casual usage. However, in scientific and formal writing, "alga" is the precise singular form.
Summary in One Paragraph

An alga is a photosynthetic, primarily water-dwelling organism that makes its own food from sunlight but lacks the roots, stems, leaves, and vascular system that true plants have. Algae range from microscopic single-celled organisms floating invisibly in the ocean to massive multicellular seaweeds stretching tens of meters long. They are not a single unified family — different types evolved separately — and they include green algae, red algae, brown algae, diatoms, and more. Despite their simplicity, algae are among the most important organisms on Earth: they produce roughly half of the planet's oxygen, anchor aquatic food chains, and are used by humans in food, industry, and medicine.
